title: Xin lỗi
summary: Different ways to say "Excuse me / sorry" in Vietnam, with the phrase to start with, reusable pieces, and related next steps.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Xin lỗi answers the traveler question "Excuse me / sorry" in small service and first-contact moments. This helps you get attention, pass by someone, or apologize for a small mistake. This is the safe all-purpose phrase for passing by, starting a question, or apologizing lightly. Its job is asking for one clear help action before adding more words. Expect a slower repeat, a pointed explanation, or a switch to writing; then use Explore next if the reply creates another small task.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Listen to each piece, then the whole phrase, so the rhythm feels connected instead of memorized word by word.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Start with Xin lỗi when "Excuse me / sorry" is the main thing you need understood. This helps you get attention, pass by someone, or apologize for a small mistake. It gives the other person room to answer with a slower repeat, a pointed explanation, or a switch to writing. Keep your voice calm and let the short phrase do the politeness work before you add another request.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.body: Polite Vietnamese often works by softening the start or end of an interaction before the main request. For "Excuse me / sorry", the useful move is asking for one clear help action before adding more words. If the first reply is still unclear, move to showing, writing, or pointing.

sections.title: Traveler insight
sections.body: In Polite Basics, locals often answer with a slower repeat, a pointed explanation, or a switch to writing rather than a long explanation. That makes Xin lỗi strongest when you say it once, pause, and let the other person show the next step. Keep your voice calm and let the short phrase do the politeness work before you add another request.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: This helps you get attention, pass by someone, or apologize for a small mistake. It fits small service and first-contact moments, especially when the next step is a slower repeat, a pointed explanation, or a switch to writing. If the first reply is still unclear, move to showing, writing, or pointing.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Keep quick service phrases clear, polite, and short. A calm short sentence usually works better than a long one said nervously.

sections.title: Local tip
sections.body: A small smile and a calm pace matter. These short phrases are often enough to make a service moment feel warmer.
